steps.prompt: Without dividing, can you tell whether $123{,}456$ is divisible by $3$? By $4$? By $9$? What do you look at?
steps.placeholder: For 3 I look at… for 4 I look at…

cards.title: The quick tests
cards.body: $2$: the last digit is even. $4$: the last two digits make a multiple of $4$. $8$: the last three digits make a multiple of $8$. $5$: the last digit is $0$ or $5$. $3$ and $9$: the digit sum is a multiple of $3$ or $9$. $11$: the alternating sum of the digits ($+ - + - \ldots$) is a multiple of $11$.

cards.title: Worked example: a missing digit
cards.problem: The four-digit number $5d48$, where $d$ is a digit, is divisible by $9$. What is $d$?

steps.text: $17 + d$ must be a multiple of $9$, and $d \leq 9$, so $17 + d = 18$ and $d = 1$.

cards.title: Combine the tests
cards.body: To test a number like $12$ or $6$, split it into parts that share no factor: $12 = 3 \times 4$ and $6 = 2 \times 3$. A number is divisible by $12$ exactly when it passes the $3$ test AND the $4$ test. (Testing $2$ and $6$ is NOT enough for $12$: $6$ passes both.)

steps.text: The digit sum is $7 + 3 + 9 + 2 = 21$, a multiple of $3$: it passes the $3$ test.

try.prompt: What is the digit sum of $7{,}392$?

steps.text: The last two digits make $92 = 4 \times 23$: it passes the $4$ test too. So $7{,}392$ is divisible by $12$ (it is $12 \times 616$).

cards.title: The common trap: the wrong pair of tests
cards.body: The parts you combine must share no common factor: $12 = 3 \times 4$ works, $12 = 2 \times 6$ doesn't. For $11$, start the alternating sum from the left with $+$, and remember that $0$ counts as a multiple of $11$. The digit-sum test only works for $3$ and $9$.

prompts: Which divisibility test do you trust most, and which one do you still mix up?
